line_style = [:solid, :dash, :dashdot]
function draw_region()
    p = plot(Shape(first.(corners), last.(corners)), color=cb_blue, alpha=0.25,
        linewidth=0, xlims=(25, 52), ylims=(15, 42), xlabel=L"R_1 \; \mathrm{[g/s]}",
        ylabel=L"R_2 \; \mathrm{[g/s]}")
    for j in 1:n_receptors
        a1, a2, rhs = boundaries[j]
        # Label each line at a point where it is inside the axes
        if abs(a2) < 1e-6

            label_at = (rhs / a1 - 1.4, 17)

    end

The Simplex Method

Walking the Corners

For simple LPs, we can just list the corners and evaluate the objective at each. This doesn’t scale.

The simplex method (Dantzig, 1963) is the core algorithm for solving LPs (assuming the problem is minimization):

  1. Start at any corner. Look along each edge neighboring it.
  2. If the objective decreases, move its other corner.
  3. Stop when the objective increases across every edge.

The Objective Along an Edge

The cost \(f = 20R_1 + 30R_2\) has gradient \(\nabla f = (20, 30)\), in $1000/yr per g/s removed.

Changing the removals by \(\mathbf{d} = (d_1, d_2)\) changes the cost by

\[\nabla f \cdot \mathbf{d} = 20\,d_1 + 30\,d_2.\]

Along an edge, the objective decreases if this is negative and increases if it is positive.

This is what “look along each edge” means in practice. The objective is linear, so its gradient is the same everywhere and the test needs only the edge’s direction, never the cost at the far corner. Take d per g/s of removal given up at one stack: (-1, 0) along the top edge, (0, -1) down the right edge. Along a receptor’s constraint, giving up 1 g/s at stack 1 has to be made up at stack 2, so d has a positive second entry. In a tableau these numbers are the reduced costs.

Step 1: Start at a Corner

Code 
# Corners next to corner k are its neighbours in order around the region
neighbours(k) = [mod1(k - 1, length(corners)), mod1(k + 1, length(corners))]

# How the removals change along the edge from corner k to corner m,
# per g/s of removal given up (or added) at one stack
function edge_direction(k, m)
    move = corners[m] .- corners[k]
    if abs(move[1]) > 1e-6
        return move ./ abs(move[1])
    end
    return move ./ abs(move[2])
end

# How fast the cost changes along that edge: the cost gradient (20, 30)
# dotted with the edge's direction
function edge_rate(k, m)
    return sum(cost .* edge_direction(k, m))
end

# The walk: from the corner that removes the most, follow the edge along
# which the cost falls fastest, and stop when no edge lowers the cost
start = argmax([sum(c) for c in corners])
path = zeros(Int, length(corners))              # at most one visit per corner
path[1] = start
n_steps = 1
while true
    here = path[n_steps]
    rates = [edge_rate(here, m) for m in neighbours(here)]
    if minimum(rates) >= 0
        break                                   # the cost rises along every edge
    end
    global n_steps += 1
    path[n_steps] = neighbours(here)[argmin(rates)]
end
path = path[1:n_steps]

# Draw the walk after `step` moves, with the costs of the corners in view
function draw_walk(step)
    p = draw_region()
    scatter!(p, first.(corners), last.(corners), color=:gray60, markersize=7,
        markerstrokecolor=:gray30)
    visited = path[1:(step + 1)]
    plot!(p, [corners[k][1] for k in visited], [corners[k][2] for k in visited],
        color=cb_vermillion, linewidth=4, arrow=true)
    here = visited[end]
    for k in [here; neighbours(here)]
        # Write each corner's cost just inside the region, toward its centre
        inward = centre .- corners[k]
        inward = 2.6 .* inward ./ sqrt(sum(inward .^ 2))
        annotate!(p, corners[k][1] + inward[1], corners[k][2] + inward[2],
            text(string(Int(round(corner_cost[k]))), 16, :black, plot_font))
    end
    scatter!(p, [corners[here][1]], [corners[here][2]], color=cb_vermillion,
        markersize=12, markerstrokecolor=:black)
    annotate!(p, 25.6, 21, text("costs in \$1000/yr", 14, :left, :black, plot_font))
    plot!(p, size=(580, 450), left_margin=5mm, bottom_margin=5mm)
    return p
end

draw_walk(0)

Start where both stacks remove all they can.

  • Left: \(\nabla f \cdot (-1, 0) = -20\)
  • Down: \(\nabla f \cdot (0, -1) = -30\)

Both edges lower the cost; down is steeper.

Step 2: Go Towards Steepest Decrease

Code 
draw_walk(1)
  • Back up: \(\nabla f \cdot (0, 1) = +30\)
  • Along C3: \(\nabla f \cdot (-1, 0.109) = -16.7\)

Simplex moved down because that edge was steeper: the cost falls 30 per g/s there against 20 along the top edge (the classic rule takes the most negative). From the new corner, going back up raises the cost, so the only candidate is the edge along C3. Staying on C3 keeps receptor C exactly at the standard, so each g/s given up at stack 1 has to be made up by about 0.11 g/s at stack 2: that saves 20 and costs about 3.3. The slide’s 0.109 comes from the unrounded transmission factors; the rounded coefficients 1.5 and 14.2 give 0.106.

Step 3: Keep Moving

Code 
draw_walk(2)
  • Back along C3: \(\nabla f \cdot (1, -0.109) = +16.7\)
  • Along C2: \(\nabla f \cdot (-1, 0.786) = +3.6\)

Along C3 the cost fell, so simplex moved to its far corner. Now test this corner’s two edges. Along C2, stack 2 has to make up about 0.79 g/s for each g/s stack 1 gives up, which costs more (about 23.6) than it saves (20). Neither edge lowers the cost.

Step 4: Stop

Along both edges leaving this corner, \(\nabla f \cdot \mathbf{d} > 0\): the cost would rise, to 1728 or 1785 from 1705.

For a linear objective, a corner with no decreasing edge is an optimum: no further walking can help. The simplex algorithm took 2 steps and never looked at several corners.

Solvers do the same walk with algebra: a tableau by hand.

Why is a local stop global? The feasible region is convex and the cost is linear, so if every edge out of a corner goes uphill, every direction into the region does too. That is the same argument as Wednesday’s “why a corner”, run in reverse.

Shadow Prices

Binding Constraints

A solution is found at a corner of the feasible region. At that corner, two or more constraints are binding: if we relaxed one by weakening it, we could improve the solution.

At our optimum, C2 and C3 bind; C1 is slack, and changing its value would not improve the solution.

Shadow Prices

The marginal cost of a constraint is the amount by which the solution would improve if the constraint capacity was relaxed by one unit.

This is also referred to as the shadow price (these are also called the dual variables of the constraint).

Non-zero shadow prices tell us that the constraint is binding, and their values rank which constraints are most influential.

Lagrange Multipliers Need Equalities

Lagrange multipliers handle equality constraints. Standard form has inequalities, so each gets a squared slack variable:

\[g_j(\mathbf{x}) \leq b_j \qquad \text{becomes} \qquad g_j(\mathbf{x}) + S_j^2 = b_j\]

  • \(S_j = 0\): constraint \(j\) is binding.
  • \(S_j \neq 0\): it is slack, with \(S_j^2\) to spare.
  • Squaring keeps the slack from going negative.

We work in Wednesday’s standard form: maximize the objective subject to less-than constraints. The Lagrangian is built for equality constraints, so the inequalities are converted first. A less-than constraint has room on its left-hand side, so the slack is added. It is written as a square so that it cannot go negative and no further inequality is needed. For C2 in standard form this reads -9.0 R_1 - 11.5 R_2 + S_2^2 = -714. It is the same slack a simplex tableau carries (s_j in the appendix), with s_j = S_j^2.

Shadow Prices Are Lagrange Multipliers

For standard form, \(\max f(\mathbf{x})\) subject to \(g_j(\mathbf{x}) + S_j^2 = b_j\), the Lagrangian weights each constraint by a multiplier \(\lambda_j\):

\[\mathcal{L} = f(\mathbf{x}) - \sum_j \lambda_j \left(g_j(\mathbf{x}) + S_j^2 - b_j\right) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b_j} = \lambda_j\]

Raising \(b_j\) by one unit relaxes constraint \(j\) and improves the objective by \(\lambda_j\): its shadow price.

With every constraint an equality, the Lagrangian applies. The shadow price was defined as the rate at which the optimal objective changes when a constraint is relaxed. In standard form a larger right-hand side is a relaxation, so that rate is the derivative with respect to b_j, which is the multiplier. This is the reason to do the calculation in standard form: the multiplier reads directly as the shadow price, with no sign to sort out.

Finding the Multipliers

At an optimum, every partial derivative of \(\mathcal{L}\) is zero:

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_i} = 0: &\quad \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_j \lambda_j \nabla g_j(\mathbf{x}) \\[0.3em] \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial S_j} = 0: &\quad 2\lambda_j S_j = 0 \end{aligned}\]

So \(\lambda_j = 0\) or \(S_j = 0\): a slack constraint has no shadow price, and only binding ones stay in the sum.

Three sets of derivatives. With respect to each decision variable: together they say the objective’s gradient is a weighted sum of the constraints’ gradients, and the weights are the multipliers. With respect to each slack variable: 2 lambda_j S_j = 0, so for every constraint either the multiplier or the slack is zero (complementary slackness); a constraint with room to spare cannot have a shadow price. With respect to each multiplier: the constraint itself, which adds nothing new. This matches the last simplex step: no edge improves the objective exactly when its gradient is a non-negative combination of the binding constraints’ gradients.

Computing the Shadow Prices

In Wednesday’s standard form, \(f = -20R_1 - 30R_2\), and each gradient is a row of coefficients. C1 is slack \((S_1 \neq 0)\), so \(\lambda_1 = 0\) and \(\nabla f = \lambda_2 \nabla g_2 + \lambda_3 \nabla g_3\):

\[\begin{pmatrix} -20 \\ -30 \end{pmatrix} = \lambda_2 \begin{pmatrix} -9.0 \\ -11.5 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda_3 \begin{pmatrix} -1.5 \\ -14.2 \end{pmatrix}\]

\[\begin{aligned} -20 &= -9.0\,\lambda_2 -1.5\,\lambda_3 \\ -30 &= -11.5\,\lambda_2 -14.2\,\lambda_3 \end{aligned} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \lambda_2 = 2.15, \quad \lambda_3 = 0.37\]

Board item. Wednesday’s lecture wrote this problem in standard form: maximize f = -20 R_1 - 30 R_2, with C2 as g_2 = -9.0 R_1 - 11.5 R_2 <= -714 and C3 as g_3 = -1.5 R_1 - 14.2 R_2 <= -447. The gradients are the coefficient pairs: (-20, -30), (-9.0, -11.5) and (-1.5, -14.2). C1, the two upper bounds and non-negativity are slack at the optimum, so their multipliers are zero. Read the vector equation one row at a time to get the two equations, one for each decision variable, and solve the 2-by-2 system. Both multipliers come out positive, which is the optimality check. Relaxing C2 by one unit raises its right-hand side from -714 to -713, which is the standard at B going up by 1 µg/m³, and raises the objective by 2.15: the cost falls by 2.15.

Reading the Shadow Prices

Constraint Shadow price Meaning
C1 0 slack: relaxing it saves nothing
C2 $2,150/yr per µg/m³ the standard at B is relaxed
C3 $370/yr per µg/m³ the standard at C is relaxed

If mitigation near receptor B (rerouting a school bus stop, say) lets regulators relax the limit there by 5 µg/m³, it is worth up to about $10,800 per year in avoided treatment.

The next slide takes up the two things that matter when reading these numbers: their units, and that they are marginal.

A Shadow Price Is a Rate

  • Units: objective units per unit of the right-hand side. For C2: $2,150/yr per µg/m³.
  • Marginal: the rate at the current optimum. It holds for small changes, while the same constraints bind.

Would relaxing the standard at B by 100 µg/m³ save 100 × $2,150?

Two points students lose marks on. Units: a shadow price is the objective’s units per unit of the constraint’s right-hand side, here dollars per year per microgram per cubic metre, so a shadow price without units cannot be compared with a cost. Marginal: it is a rate at the current optimum, and it holds only while the same constraints bind. Ask the question before showing the next slide. For this problem the answer is no: the price for C2 holds until the standard at B has been relaxed by about 50 µg/m³. Past that, C1 and C3 bind, and relaxing C2 further saves nothing. The homework asks them to find a change like this in its own LP.

A Shadow Price Holds Locally

Code 
# Wednesday's sketch LP: four constraint lines, each x2 = slope * x1 + intercept.
# We minimize x1 + 2 x2 and relax the third constraint by lowering its intercept.
sketch_slope = [4.5, -1, -1.5, 0.5]
sketch_intercept = [0, 16, 12, 0]
relaxed_by = [0, 4, 14]
relaxed_style = [:solid, :dashdot, :dot]
relaxed_name = ["1: now", "2: relaxed a little", "3: relaxed a lot"]

# Where constraint lines i and k cross
function sketch_crossing(i, k)
    x1 = (sketch_intercept[k] - sketch_intercept[i]) / (sketch_slope[i] - sketch_slope[k])
    return (x1, sketch_slope[i] * x1 + sketch_intercept[i])
end

# The optimum after relaxing the third constraint: it slides down the fourth
# line until the first and fourth lines meet, and can go no further
function sketch_optimum(relaxation)
    corner = sketch_crossing(1, 4)
    x1 = (sketch_intercept[3] - relaxation) / (sketch_slope[4] - sketch_slope[3])
    if x1 <= corner[1]
        return corner
    end
    return (x1, sketch_slope[4] * x1)
end

sketch_objective(point) = point[1] + 2 * point[2]

# Left: the feasible region now (darker) and after a large relaxation (lighter)
now_region = [sketch_crossing(1, 3), sketch_crossing(1, 2), sketch_crossing(2, 4),
    sketch_crossing(4, 3)]
largest_region = [sketch_crossing(1, 4), sketch_crossing(1, 2), sketch_crossing(2, 4)]
sketch_x1 = -3:0.5:14
p_move = plot(Shape(first.(largest_region), last.(largest_region)), color=cb_blue, alpha=0.1,
    linewidth=0, xlims=(-3, 14), ylims=(-3, 16), ticks=false, xlabel=L"x_1", ylabel=L"x_2",
    legend=:topright, legendfontsize=13)
plot!(p_move, Shape(first.(now_region), last.(now_region)), color=cb_blue, alpha=0.25,
    linewidth=0)
for i in [1, 2, 4]
    plot!(p_move, sketch_x1, sketch_slope[i] .* sketch_x1 .+ sketch_intercept[i],
        color=:gray30, linewidth=2.5)
end
for k in 1:length(relaxed_by)
    plot!(p_move, sketch_x1, sketch_slope[3] .* sketch_x1 .+ sketch_intercept[3] .- relaxed_by[k],
        color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=relaxed_style[k], linewidth=2.5, label=relaxed_name[k])
    best = sketch_optimum(relaxed_by[k])
    scatter!(p_move, [best[1]], [best[2]], color=cb_vermillion, markersize=9,
        markerstrokecolor=:black)
    annotate!(p_move, best[1] + 0.9, best[2] - 1.1, text(string(k), 18, :black, plot_font))
end

# Right: the optimal objective against the relaxation, and what the shadow price predicts
relaxation = 0:0.5:16
actual = [sketch_objective(sketch_optimum(r)) for r in relaxation]
predicted = sketch_objective(sketch_optimum(0)) .- relaxation
p_value = plot(relaxation, predicted, color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dash, linewidth=2.5,
    ticks=false, xlims=(-1, 17), ylims=(-5.5, 13.5),
    xlabel="How far the constraint is relaxed", ylabel="Optimal cost")
plot!(p_value, relaxation, actual, color=:black, linewidth=3)
for k in 1:length(relaxed_by)
    value_k = sketch_objective(sketch_optimum(relaxed_by[k]))
    scatter!(p_value, [relaxed_by[k]], [value_k], color=cb_vermillion, markersize=9,
        markerstrokecolor=:black)
    annotate!(p_value, relaxed_by[k] + 0.5, value_k + 1.2, text(string(k), 18, :black, plot_font))
end
annotate!(p_value, 12.6, -3, text("the shadow price predicts", 15, :right, :black, plot_font))
annotate!(p_value, 16.6, 4, text("re-solving gives", 15, :right, :black, plot_font))

plot(p_move, p_value, layout=(1, 2), size=(1150, 310), left_margin=12mm, bottom_margin=8mm)

From 1 to 2 the same constraints bind, so the shadow price holds. By 3 the relaxed constraint no longer binds, and it fails.

This is Wednesday’s sketch with an objective added: minimize a cost that rises with both variables, so the optimum is the lowest corner. One constraint is relaxed twice. At first the optimum slides along the neighbouring constraint, the same two constraints bind, and the objective falls at a constant rate: the shadow price. Relax far enough and the optimum reaches the corner where two other constraints meet. The relaxed constraint has moved off the feasible region, a different pair of constraints sets the optimum, and further relaxation gains nothing. On the right, the solid line is what re-solving gives and the dashed line is what the shadow price predicts; they part at the kink. A shadow price cannot tell you where its own kink is: you have to re-solve.

Solving LPs in JuMP

The Same Problem in JuMP

emissions_model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
@variable(emissions_model, 0 <= removal[i in 1:n_stacks] <= emission[i])
@objective(emissions_model, Min, sum(cost[i] * removal[i] for i in 1:n_stacks))
@constraint(emissions_model, limit[j in 1:n_receptors],
    sum(t[j, i] * (emission[i] - removal[i]) for i in 1:n_stacks) <= standard)
set_silent(emissions_model)
optimize!(emissions_model)

println("Removals: ", value.(removal), " g/s")
println("Cost: \$", objective_value(emissions_model), " thousand per year")
Removals: [45.2288960384697, 26.672101520238556] g/s
Cost: $1704.7409663765507 thousand per year

The corner we walked to: 45.2 and 26.7 g/s, at about $1.7 million per year.

value.(removal) asks for the optimal value of every removal at once (value(removal[1]) for one of them), and objective_value(model) for the optimal cost. The printed numbers are unrounded, which is what students will see in their own notebooks; round when reporting. set_silent only hides the solver’s log. Monday’s lab uses the same three calls.

Reading the Duals

limit_prices = shadow_price.(limit)
JuMP By hand
C1 0.0 0
C2 -2.15 2.15
C3 -0.37 0.37

Same size, opposite sign: one objective is the negative of the other.

  • By hand, in standard form, we maximized \(-\)cost. Relaxing C2 raises that by \(+2.15\).
  • JuMP minimized cost. Relaxing C2 changes it by \(-2.15\).

Both numbers answer the same question, what happens to the objective when the constraint is relaxed by one unit, and they differ in sign only because the two objectives do. By hand we used standard form and maximized minus the cost, so relaxing C2 raises the objective by 2.15. The JuMP model on the previous slide minimizes the cost itself, so relaxing C2 lowers its objective by 2.15, and shadow_price reports minus 2.15. JuMP’s rule is that shadow_price is the change in the objective when the constraint is relaxed: never positive for a minimization, never negative for a maximization, however the constraint is written. Given the standard-form model (maximize minus the cost), JuMP returns plus 2.15 and plus 0.37, the by-hand values. The lesson for students: say what the objective is, which direction the constraint moves, and the units.

Check It: Re-solve

# Relax C2, the standard at receptor B, by 1 µg/m³ and solve again
base_cost = objective_value(emissions_model)
set_normalized_rhs(limit[2], normalized_rhs(limit[2]) + 1)
optimize!(emissions_model)
relaxed_cost = objective_value(emissions_model)
println("Removals: ", value.(removal), " g/s")
println("Cost: \$", relaxed_cost, " thousand per year")
println("Change in cost: ", relaxed_cost - base_cost)
Removals: [45.100241061880524, 26.686075542467893] g/s
Cost: $1702.5870875116473 thousand per year
Change in cost: -2.1538788649033904

The cost changes by -2.15 ($1000/yr): the shadow price of C2, as promised.

This is the verification step: the shadow price is a prediction about re-solving, so re-solve and check. The printed removals show the plan shifting slightly, not only the cost. A hidden cell after this one sets the right-hand side back, which students should also do before reusing a model they have changed. It matches to the digits shown because a 1 µg/m³ change does not change which constraints bind. A large enough change would, and then the shadow price would stop predicting the new cost.

Key Takeaways and Upcoming Schedule

Key Takeaways

  • Simplex walks downhill from corner to corner and stops when no edge improves.
  • At the optimum, binding constraints hold exactly; slack ones have room to spare.
  • A shadow price is how much the objective improves per unit a constraint is relaxed. Zero means slack.
  • Read shadow prices with units, and check the solver’s sign convention.

Appendix

A Simplex Tableau by Hand

Easiest when the origin is a feasible corner:

\[\begin{aligned} \max_{x_1, x_2} \quad & 230x_1 + 120x_2 \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & 0.9x_1 + 0.5x_2 + s_1 = 600, \quad x_1 + x_2 + s_2 = 1000 \end{aligned}\]

At the origin, \(s_1 = 600\) and \(s_2 = 1000\).

  • Entering: \(x_1\), the largest objective coefficient (230).
  • Leaving: \(s_1\), by the ratio test \(\min(600/0.9,\ 1000)\).

A Simplex Tableau by Hand

\[z = 153333 - 7.8\,x_2 - 255.6\,s_1\]

Every coefficient is negative, so no pivot can raise \(z\): optimal at \(x_1 =\) 666.7 and \(x_2 = 0\).

The coefficient of each slack is that constraint’s shadow price: about 255.6 for the first, 0 for the second (its slack is still positive).
